How Kotlin calls Apple

In iosMain, your Kotlin can call Apple's own code, like the class that knows the operating system's name. But Apple's code isn't Kotlin. Here's how Kotlin/Native makes it callable.

The problem

Puzzle 1 said iosMain can use what only iOS has. On iOS, the operating system's name and version come from an Apple class called UIDevice. Apple wrote it for its own languages, not for Kotlin. So how can a Kotlin file in iosMain call it?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Apple's code is grouped into frameworks: bundles of ready-made code for one area. Foundation has basics like dates, text and unique IDs; UIKit has everything about screens, including UIDevice.

Kotlin can't read those frameworks directly. So Kotlin/Native ships platform libraries: prebuilt Kotlin descriptions, called bindings, of each target's native libraries. For Apple targets they cover Apple's frameworks. The packages are there by default, under platform.:

// iosMain
import platform.UIKit.UIDevice

fun systemName(): String = UIDevice.currentDevice.systemName()

The binding tells Kotlin what the call is named, what it accepts, and what it returns. The implementation belongs to UIKit. When you build, Kotlin/Native records the connection to UIKit so the call can reach Apple's code when the app runs.

Two consequences:

  • These bindings exist only for Apple targets. That's why import platform.UIKit works in iosMain and fails in commonMain (puzzle 1's rule: common code may use only what every target has).
  • The names and shapes are Apple's, not Kotlin's: UIDevice.currentDevice reads a little foreign. That's normal.

The analogy

A phrasebook for a country whose language you don't speak. You don't learn the language; you look up the phrase and say it, and you're understood. Each target comes with its own phrasebook, and the Apple one only works in Apple's countries.

Who wrote the Kotlin binding for UIDevice?

Not quite. Apple doesn't; the Kotlin/Native distribution includes them.

Not quite. You don't have to; Apple's bindings come prebuilt.

Right. Prebuilt, shipped with Kotlin/Native.

These are called platform libraries. The packages from platform libraries are available by default"; "The Kotlin/Native compiler automatically detects which platform libraries are accessed and links the necessary ones")

What you now know

Kotlin/Native ships platform libraries: prebuilt Kotlin bindings for each target's native libraries. On Apple targets they cover Apple's frameworks, such as Foundation and UIKit, so code in iosMain can import platform.UIKit.UIDevice and call it like Kotlin. They exist only on Apple targets, which is why such calls live in iosMain, never in commonMain.
